about: Researched oldest everyday things found or made in the British Isles (clothing and shoes, tools, boats and wheels, coins, jewellery and clocks), each with quoted sources; researched 2026-10-27.

entries.name: Orkney Hood
entries.claim: Described by National Museums Scotland as the only complete piece of clothing to survive from before the medieval period in Scotland
entries.evidence: The child-sized woollen hood with a tablet-woven fringe was found in a peat bog at Tankerness, Orkney, in 1867. It was long thought Viking-age until a radiocarbon date of 1991 placed it between AD 250 and 615, in the Late Iron Age; its cloth was cut down from older garments. Fragments of older textiles survive elsewhere in the isles, so the claim is for a complete garment.

sources.title: Orkney Hood
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Radiocarbon testing dated the hood to some point between 250 and 615 CE.

entries.name: Bronze Age toddler's shoe from north Kent
entries.claim: May be the oldest shoe found in the British Isles
entries.evidence: A 15 cm leather shoe sole found by a mudlark on a north Kent foreshore in 2022 was radiocarbon dated twice to 888–781 BC; the previous record-holder, found in a hollow tree at Whiteball quarry in Somerset in 2005, is about 2,000 years old. The finder has not named the beach, the shoe has not yet been fully published, and the claim is the finders' own ('pretty confident').

entries.name: Happisburgh flint tools
entries.claim: The oldest human artefacts found in Britain
entries.evidence: Seventy-eight worked flints excavated on the foreshore at Happisburgh, Norfolk, and published in 2010 come from sediments laid down in one of two warm periods, about 840,000 or 950,000 years ago. That is at least 100,000 years earlier than the tools from Pakefield, Suffolk. No human remains were found, so the makers are unknown (Homo antecessor is suggested).

entries.name: Clacton Spear
entries.age_text: c. 400,000 years ago (420,000 on the museum label)
entries.claim: The oldest worked wooden implement found in Britain, and a contender for the oldest wooden weapon in the world
entries.evidence: The tip of a yew spear was found at Clacton-on-Sea, Essex, in 1911 in deposits of the Hoxnian interglacial. It has been called the oldest known worked wooden weapon, but archaeologists count it, the Schöningen spears of Germany and the Kathu Pan points of South Africa as contenders for the oldest evidence of weapons, and it was once thought to be a digging stick.

sources.quote: at approximately 400,000 years old, it is the oldest known worked wooden weapon

entries.name: Rotten Bottom bow
entries.claim: The oldest bow found in Britain
entries.evidence: Half of a yew flatbow was found by a hill walker in 1990 in the peat at Rotten Bottom, Tweedsmuir, in the Scottish Borders, and radiocarbon dated to 4040–3640 BC, in the early Neolithic. It is older than Ötzi's bow from the Alps; a yew bow from Somerset is dated 2700–2600 BC. Bows of this age are very rare in Britain and Ireland.

sources.quote: A slightly shorter bow comes from the Scottish parish of Tweedsmuir in a peat bog known as Rotten Bottom.

entries.name: Must Farm wheel
entries.claim: The earliest and most complete wheel found in Britain
entries.evidence: A wooden wheel about a metre across, with its hub, was found in 2016 at the Must Farm pile-dwelling settlement near Peterborough, which burned and sank into a river channel in the Late Bronze Age. A horse's spine found nearby suggests a horse-drawn cart. Wheels were in use on the Continent much earlier, so the record is for Britain.

sources.title: Must Farm Bronze Age settlement

sources.quote: represents the most complete and earliest of its type found in Britain

entries.name: Kentish cast bronzes ('Thurrock' potins)
entries.claim: The first coins made in Britain
entries.evidence: Gold coins from Gaul were imported in numbers from about 150 BC; the first coins made in Britain seem to be cast bronze (potin) pieces copying the Apollo-and-bull bronzes of Massalia (Marseille), circulating mainly in Kent at the end of the 2nd century BC. Whether they were cast in Kent, on the north bank of the Thames or in Gaul is debated, and dates vary from about 150 to 100 BC. Iron currency bars were used before coins.

entries.name: Hiberno-Norse pennies of Sihtric Silkbeard
entries.claim: The first coins struck in Ireland
entries.evidence: Silver pennies copying those of Æthelred II of England were struck in Dublin for the Norse king Sihtric III (Silkbeard) from about 997 or 998. For about a century before, coins made elsewhere (Anglo-Saxon, Carolingian and Islamic) had circulated in Viking Ireland. Some sources put the first issue a year or two earlier.

entries.name: Silver pennies of David I
entries.claim: The first coins of the Kingdom of Scotland
entries.evidence: David I struck silver pennies after taking Carlisle, with its English mint and the silver mines at Alston, in 1136; the first were close copies of King Stephen's pennies. Roman and other foreign coins had circulated in Scotland long before. The 1136 start is the traditional date.

entries.name: Star Carr pendant
entries.claim: The earliest known Mesolithic art in Britain
entries.evidence: A small engraved shale pendant, 31 by 35 mm, was found in 2015 at the Early Mesolithic lakeside site of Star Carr, North Yorkshire. No other engraved shale pendant is known in Europe. The claim is for the Mesolithic: older, Palaeolithic art is known in Britain.

entries.name: Amesbury Archer's gold hair ornaments
entries.age_text: as early as 2470 BC; burial c. 2300 BC
entries.claim: The earliest gold objects found in Britain
entries.evidence: A pair of small gold hair tresses (sometimes called earrings) was buried with the 'Amesbury Archer', a man who died around 2300 BC near Stonehenge, in the richest early Bronze Age grave found in Britain; the gold has been dated as early as 2470 BC. Wikipedia words the record for England, Wessex Archaeology for Britain.

sources.title: Amesbury Archer
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a pair of gold hair ornaments, the oldest gold objects known from England

sources.title: The Amesbury Archer
sources.author: Wessex Archaeology
sources.quote: The gold dated to as early as 2,470BC and is the earliest found in Britain.

entries.name: Llanllyfni lunula
entries.claim: One of the earliest gold ornaments from Wales
entries.evidence: A crescent-shaped gold collar found in a bog on Llecheiddior-uchaf farm near Llanllyfni, Gwynedd, about 1869; at 185 g it is the heaviest lunula from Britain and Ireland. Lunulae are not directly dated: a box with an Irish one gives 2460–2040 BC, and most of the hundred or so known come from Ireland. Museum Wales lists it among the items stolen from a Cardiff museum, so where it is now is uncertain.

entries.name: Salisbury Cathedral clock
entries.claim: Said to be the oldest working mechanical clock in the world
entries.evidence: A dial-less iron-framed verge-and-foliot clock, rediscovered in the cathedral in 1928 and restored to working order in 1956; it is identified with a clock mentioned in a deed of 1386. Its construction has been compared with much later clocks, so some doubt that it is the 1386 clock, and Beauvais, Chioggia and Comayagua make rival claims; its escapement is said to have been replaced in the 17th century.

entries.name: Wells Cathedral clock
entries.claim: Its astronomical dial is claimed as the oldest surviving original clock face anywhere
entries.evidence: The clock in the north transept shows the sun and moon circling a fixed earth, with jousting knights that turn at each quarter. Its original works, dated between 1386 and 1392, were replaced in the 19th century and now run in the Science Museum in London; the face is still in the cathedral. The cathedral itself calls the mechanism the second oldest in Britain, after Salisbury, and the face claim is its own.
